title: Anatomy and Physiology – SPČR 2018 Exam Tests
description: Exam questions on anatomy and physiology for divers

questions.question: The body obtains its energy:
questions.explanation: The body obtains energy from nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins), which are processed via metabolism. Breathing is the process that supplies the oxygen needed for this conversion.

questions.question: The most readily available energy source is:
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the most readily available energy source because they break down fastest and release energy quickly. Fats provide more energy, but take longer to process.

questions.question: The digestive system does NOT include:
questions.explanation: The larynx is part of the respiratory system, not the digestive one. The teeth, pharynx and oesophagus belong to the digestive tract.

questions.question: The thoracic cavity is separated from the abdominal cavity by:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is the flat muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. It is essential for breathing — on inhalation it contracts and the lungs expand.

questions.question: The vestibular organ is located:
questions.explanation: The vestibular organ (balance organ) sits in the inner ear together with the hearing organ. Divers should know that equalisation problems can therefore affect balance.

questions.question: The proportion of water in an adult's total body mass is:
questions.explanation: The human body contains roughly 60% water. This matters for understanding diving physiology, including dehydration and inert-gas on-gassing of tissues.

questions.question: The absorption of nutrients from food takes place mainly:
questions.explanation: Most nutrient absorption takes place in the small intestine, which has a large surface area thanks to its villi. Digestion happens mainly in the stomach; the large intestine mainly absorbs water.

questions.question: The proportion of water in an adult's total body mass is:
questions.explanation: The human body contains roughly 60% water. This question is the same as question 6 with the answer order reshuffled.

questions.question: The space between the lens and the retina of the eye is filled with:
questions.explanation: The vitreous humour is a transparent jelly-like substance that fills the space between the lens and the retina. It maintains the shape of the eyeball and lets light pass through.

questions.question: The basic vital functions are:
questions.explanation: The basic vital functions are consciousness, breathing and circulation. Checking each is essential in first aid — if any is missing, immediate action is required.

questions.question: The kidneys are part of the:
questions.explanation: The kidneys are the main organ of the excretory system. They filter blood and remove waste products from the body as urine.

questions.question: The cornea is part of:
questions.explanation: The cornea is the transparent front part of the eye that refracts light and protects the inner structures.

questions.question: The inner ear contains:

options.text: the auditory (Eustachian) tube and the external auditory canal
the auditory (Eustachian) tube and the eardrum

questions.explanation: The inner ear contains the auditory organ (cochlea) and the vestibular organ (balance organ). The auditory ossicles are in the middle ear.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The basic vital functions are consciousness, breathing and circulation.
The eyeball is filled with vitreous humour.
Deoxygenated blood returns to the heart through the portal vein.
By respiratory gases we mean oxygen and carbon dioxide.

questions.explanation: Statement (c) is incorrect — deoxygenated blood returns to the heart through the superior and inferior vena cava, not the portal vein, which carries blood from the digestive tract to the liver.

questions.question: The human musculoskeletal system is made up of:
questions.explanation: The musculoskeletal system consists of the skeletal system (bones, joints) and the muscular system. The nervous system controls movement but is not part of the musculoskeletal system.

questions.question: Blood:

options.text: removes metabolic waste products from tissues

questions.explanation: Blood does all of the above — it transports oxygen and carbon dioxide, hormones and metabolic waste.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a basic vital function?
questions.explanation: The basic vital functions are consciousness, breathing and circulation. Digestion is not among them — a person can survive days or weeks without food.

questions.question: The oesophagus opens into:
questions.explanation: The oesophagus connects the pharynx to the stomach. The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, which follows the stomach.

questions.question: The auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) are located:
questions.explanation: The auditory ossicles sit in the middle ear and transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the inner ear. Equalisation of middle-ear pressure is critical for divers.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: Blood breaks food down into nutrients.
Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.
Blood is involved in regulating body temperature.
Blood transports carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs.

questions.explanation: Statement (a) is incorrect — blood does not break down food; that is the digestive system's job. Blood only transports nutrients once they have been absorbed.

questions.question: Inside the pleural space there is:
questions.explanation: The pleural space (between the visceral and parietal pleura) holds a slight negative pressure, which keeps the lungs expanded and allows breathing.

questions.question: On a breath-hold dive, the air pressure in the lungs and airways is:

options.text: the same as the surface pressure
the same as the ambient pressure

questions.explanation: When diving with scuba, the air pressure in the lungs is always equal to the ambient pressure. This is what the regulator delivers.

questions.question: The volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation is called:
questions.explanation: Vital lung capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation. In an adult it is approximately 4–5 litres.

questions.question: The larynx is part of:
questions.explanation: The larynx is part of the upper airways. It contains the vocal cords and connects the pharynx to the trachea.

questions.question: The volume of air that cannot be exhaled even with forceful exhalation is called:
questions.explanation: Residual lung volume is the air that remains in the lungs even after a maximum exhalation. It is approximately 1.5 litres.

questions.question: Residual lung volume is the volume of air:

options.text: in which no exchange of respiratory gases occurs
that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation
that cannot be exhaled even by forceful exhalation
that lies between the parietal and visceral pleurae

questions.explanation: Residual lung volume is the air that cannot be exhaled even with maximum forceful exhalation. It is important for breath-hold dive calculations.

questions.question: The diaphragm plays a major role in:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle. On inhalation it contracts and moves down, increasing thoracic-cavity volume and drawing air into the lungs.

questions.question: The negative pressure in the pleural space:
questions.explanation: The negative pressure in the pleural space keeps the lungs expanded. In a pneumothorax (air entering the pleural space) the lung can collapse.

questions.question: The lungs are kept expanded by:

options.text: the negative pressure in the pleural space
the partial pressure of carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: The lungs are kept expanded by the negative pressure in the pleural space. Their own elasticity would actually pull them inward.

questions.question: The anatomical dead space of the airways is approximately:
questions.explanation: The anatomical dead space (where no gas exchange occurs) is approximately 0.15 litre (150 mL). Diving equipment increases this dead space.

questions.question: The residual lung volume is approximately:
questions.explanation: The residual lung volume is approximately 1.5 litres. This is the air that remains in the lungs even after a maximum exhalation.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The respiratory system consists of the airways and the lungs.
The parietal pleura covers the surface of the lungs.
Total lung volume is the sum of vital capacity and residual volume.
The anatomical dead space is approximately 0.15 litre.

questions.explanation: Statement (b) is incorrect — the surface of the lungs is covered by the visceral pleura (poplicnice). The parietal pleura (pohrudnice) lines the chest wall.

questions.question: Vital lung capacity is the volume of air:

options.text: in which no exchange of respiratory gases occurs
that lies between the visceral and parietal pleurae
that cannot be exhaled even by forceful exhalation
that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation

questions.explanation: Vital lung capacity is the volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation. In an adult it is approximately 4–5 litres.

questions.question: Total lung volume is the sum of:

options.text: vital capacity and anatomical dead space
residual volume and expiratory reserve volume
residual volume and anatomical dead space

questions.explanation: Total lung volume = vital capacity + residual volume. In an adult that is approximately 6 litres (4.5 L vital capacity + 1.5 L residual volume).

questions.question: Anatomical dead space refers to:

options.text: the volume of air that remains in the lungs even after forceful exhalation
the volume in which no gas exchange occurs
the difference between a normal and a maximum inhalation
the difference between maximum inhalation and maximum exhalation lung volumes

questions.explanation: Dead space is the part of the airway (nose, larynx, trachea, bronchi) where no gas exchange takes place. Exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.question: The airways include:
questions.explanation: The airways include the bronchi and bronchioles. Alveoli are part of the lungs themselves; pulmonary blood vessels are part of the circulatory system.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the respiratory system?
questions.explanation: The oesophagus is part of the digestive system, not the respiratory one. It runs alongside the trachea and connects the pharynx to the stomach.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The pleural space lies between the visceral pleura (the lung surface) and the parietal pleura (the chest-wall lining).
There is a negative pressure in the pleural space.
The lungs sit on either side of the mediastinum.
The lungs are kept expanded by their own elasticity.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — the lungs are kept expanded by the negative pressure in the pleural space, not by their own elasticity. Lung elasticity would actually pull them inward.

questions.question: Alveoli:

options.text: are about a quarter of a millimetre in diameter
lie at the end of the airways
are surrounded by a network of capillaries

questions.explanation: All statements are correct. Alveoli are tiny sacs at the end of the airways, surrounded by capillaries, where respiratory-gas exchange takes place.

questions.question: The airways begin at:
questions.explanation: The airways begin in the nasal cavity (and the oral cavity). Air then continues through the pharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchi to the alveoli.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The aorta carries blood out of the left ventricle.

questions.explanation: Statement (a) is incorrect — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Arteries are defined by direction of flow (away from the heart), not by oxygenation.

questions.question: The pulmonary artery carries:

options.text: deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the lungs
oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
deoxygenated blood from the lungs to the right atrium

questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, where the blood is oxygenated. It is the only artery carrying deoxygenated blood.

questions.question: An adult has approximately:
questions.explanation: An adult has approximately 5–6 litres of blood, which represents about 7–8% of body mass.

questions.question: An adult heart pumps 5 litres of blood at rest in approximately:
questions.explanation: The heart pumps approximately 5 litres of blood per minute at rest (cardiac output). Under exertion this can rise to 25–30 litres.

questions.question: Oxygenated blood is delivered from the lungs:
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. From there it goes to the left ventricle and out via the aorta to the rest of the body.

questions.question: Blood ejected from the right ventricle is:

options.text: ejected to the head, trunk and limbs

questions.explanation: The right ventricle ejects deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it is oxygenated.

questions.question: Deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation is delivered:
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the superior and inferior vena cava to the right atrium. From there it goes to the right ventricle and on to the lungs.

questions.question: The resting heart rate of a healthy adult is approximately:
questions.explanation: The resting heart rate of a healthy adult is approximately 60–80 beats per minute, typically around 70. In trained athletes it can be lower.

questions.question: The pulmonary (lesser) circulation is the loop:

options.text: from the left ventricle through the lungs to the right atrium
from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left atrium
from the left ventricle through the left atrium and lungs to the right atrium
from the right atrium through the lungs to the right ventricle

questions.explanation: Pulmonary (lesser) circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Its purpose is to oxygenate the blood.

questions.question: The aorta:

options.text: is part of the systemic circulation

questions.explanation: All statements are correct. The aorta is the largest artery in the body; it leaves the left ventricle and distributes oxygenated blood to the rest of the body (the systemic circulation).

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle into the systemic circulation.
The heart pumps approximately 5 litres of blood per minute at rest.
The pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs.
Oxygenated blood is delivered to the right atrium.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — oxygenated blood is delivered to the left atrium (from the lungs). The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body.

questions.question: The aorta:

options.text: is part of the pulmonary circulation

questions.explanation: Only answer (c) is correct — the aorta carries oxygenated blood. It leaves the left ventricle (not the right) and is part of the systemic circulation (not the pulmonary one).

questions.question: The most extensively branched part of the circulatory system is formed by:
questions.explanation: Capillaries form the most branched network of the circulatory system. Their total length in the human body is estimated at 100,000 km.

questions.question: The smallest blood vessels are:
questions.explanation: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, with a diameter of about 5–10 micrometres. Their wall is a single layer of cells, which allows substances to be exchanged with the surrounding tissues.

questions.question: An adult heart pumps at rest, in 1 minute, approximately:
questions.explanation: Cardiac output at rest is approximately 5 litres per minute. That means the entire blood volume passes through the heart roughly once per minute.

questions.question: Deoxygenated blood is carried to the lungs:

options.text: by the aorta from the left ventricle
by the pulmonary artery from the right ventricle

questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood is carried to the lungs by the pulmonary artery (truncus pulmonalis) from the right ventricle. In the lungs the blood is oxygenated.

questions.question: The portal vein carries blood:

options.text: from the abdominal organs to the liver
from the lungs to the liver
from the liver to the kidneys
from the heart into the systemic circulation

questions.explanation: The portal vein (vena portae) carries blood from the digestive tract and spleen to the liver. The liver then processes the nutrients absorbed from the intestines.

questions.question: The pulmonary artery:

options.text: is part of the pulmonary circulation

questions.explanation: All statements are correct. The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle, carries deoxygenated blood and is part of the pulmonary (lesser) circulation.

questions.question: Blood ejected from the right ventricle goes:
questions.explanation: Blood from the right ventricle is ejected through the pulmonary artery into the pulmonary circulation, where it is oxygenated in the lungs.

questions.question: Under exertion, an adult heart pumps in 1 minute:
questions.explanation: Under intense exertion, cardiac output can rise to 25–30 litres per minute (in trained athletes). At rest it is approximately 5 litres.

questions.question: The main stimulus to inhale is irritation of the respiratory centre by:

options.text: lack of oxygen in the body
lack of carbon dioxide in the body
excess carbon dioxide in the body

questions.explanation: The main stimulus to inhale is a rising CO₂ level in the blood. That is why hyperventilation is dangerous — it lowers CO₂, so the diver may not feel the urge to breathe.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide passes from tissues into blood and from blood into the lungs:

options.text: due to an increased partial pressure of nitrogen
by diffusion driven by partial-pressure differences
through the action of white blood cells

questions.explanation: Gas exchange occurs by diffusion — gases move from the area with higher partial pressure to the area with lower partial pressure.

questions.question: An adult takes, at rest in 1 minute, approximately:
questions.explanation: Resting respiratory rate in an adult is approximately 12–20 breaths per minute, typically around 16.

questions.question: Blood plasma:

options.text: carries red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets

questions.explanation: All statements are correct. Blood plasma is a yellowish liquid that makes up about 55% of blood volume, contains 90% water and carries the blood cells.

questions.question: Respiratory gases are:
questions.explanation: Respiratory gases are oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) — the gases exchanged between the body and its environment during breathing.

questions.question: Blood plasma:

options.text: binds oxygen by a reversible chemical bond
is produced in the bone marrow

questions.explanation: Only (b) is correct. Oxygen is bound by haemoglobin in red blood cells (not by plasma); the bone marrow produces blood cells, not plasma.

questions.question: Red blood cells are produced:

options.text: in the blood from blood plasma

questions.explanation: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are produced in the red bone marrow. In adults, mainly in the flat bones (pelvis, sternum, skull).

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: White blood cells are involved in stopping bleeding.
Red blood cells are produced in the bone marrow.

questions.explanation: Statement (a) is incorrect — bleeding is stopped by platelets (thrombocytes), not by white blood cells. White cells fight infection.

questions.question: For oxygen transport, the most important property of blood is:

options.text: the presence of white blood cells
the ability to bind oxygen by a reversible chemical bond

questions.explanation: Oxygen transport relies on the ability of haemoglobin in red blood cells to bind oxygen reversibly — picking it up in the lungs and releasing it in the tissues.

questions.question: Oxygen is transported by:
questions.explanation: Oxygen is transported by red blood cells (erythrocytes), which contain haemoglobin — the oxygen-binding pigment.

questions.question: Oxygen binds to haemoglobin via:
questions.explanation: Oxygen binds to haemoglobin via a reversible chemical bond. In the lungs (high <var>p</var><sub>O₂</sub>) it binds, in the tissues (low <var>p</var><sub>O₂</sub>) it is released. Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly, which is why it is so toxic.

questions.question: Platelets are involved in:
questions.explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes) are involved in stopping bleeding — they aggregate at sites of vessel injury and contribute to clot formation.

questions.question: White blood cells are involved in:
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system and protect the body against infection — they destroy bacteria, viruses and other pathogens.

questions.question: Red blood cells are involved in:
questions.explanation: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin and their main role is to transport oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and CO₂ back to the lungs.

questions.question: Internal respiration is the exchange of respiratory gases:

options.text: between the surroundings and the lungs

questions.explanation: Internal (tissue) respiration is the exchange of gases between blood and tissues. Oxygen passes from blood into the cells; CO₂ goes the other way.

questions.question: External respiration is the exchange of respiratory gases:

options.text: between the surroundings and the lungs

questions.explanation: External (pulmonary) respiration is the exchange of gases between the alveoli and the blood in the pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen passes into the blood; CO₂ into the alveoli.

questions.question: The respiratory centre is located:
questions.explanation: The respiratory centre lies in the medulla oblongata. It mainly responds to blood CO₂ levels and controls the rate and depth of breathing.

questions.question: Alveolar air at normal pressure contains approximately:

options.text: 21% oxygen and 0.03% carbon dioxide on inhalation, 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide on exhalation

questions.explanation: Alveolar air contains approximately 15% O₂ and 5% CO₂. It differs from inhaled air (21% O₂, 0.03% CO₂) because gas exchange takes place there.

questions.question: An adult inhales at rest, per breath:
questions.explanation: Resting tidal volume is approximately 0.5 litre (500 mL). It rises during exertion. Vital capacity (a maximum inhalation) is 4–5 litres.

questions.question: Oxygen passes from the lungs into the blood and from the blood into the tissues:

options.text: due to an increased partial pressure of nitrogen
by being displaced by carbon dioxide
by diffusion driven by partial-pressure differences

questions.explanation: Oxygen moves by diffusion from areas of higher partial pressure (lungs, blood) to areas of lower partial pressure (blood, tissues).

questions.question: The paranasal sinuses are connected to:
questions.explanation: The paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary) are connected to the nasal cavity. While diving the pressure equalises in them automatically.

questions.question: In a healthy person the paranasal sinuses are:

options.text: freely connected to the middle-ear cavities
freely connected to the nasal cavity
connected to the airways through a one-way valve

questions.explanation: In a healthy person, the paranasal sinuses are freely connected to the nasal cavity, so pressure equalises automatically. With a cold the connection can become narrowed.

questions.question: The onset of nitrogen narcosis is marked by:
questions.explanation: The onset of nitrogen narcosis (rapture of the deep) is typically marked by euphoria and a sense of exhilaration, similar to drunkenness. This is dangerous because the diver may not recognise the problem.

questions.question: The onset of nitrogen narcosis can be hastened by:
questions.explanation: All of these can hasten the onset of narcosis: stress, exertion, poor breathing technique (CO₂ build-up), as well as fatigue, cold or alcohol.

questions.question: Long-term immersion without an insulating suit is possible in water of at least:
questions.explanation: Long-term immersion without a wetsuit requires water of at least about 35 °C (the thermoneutral zone). Water removes heat 25× faster than air.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a body response to cold?
questions.explanation: Exhilaration (euphoria) is not a response to cold. Vasoconstriction, immersion polyuria and shivering are all typical defensive responses to cold.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: Carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as carbonates.
Forced over-breathing (hyperventilation) leads to a build-up of oxygen in the body.
External respiration is the exchange of gases between the lungs and the blood.
Internal respiration is the exchange of gases between the blood and the tissues.

questions.explanation: Statement (b) is incorrect — hyperventilation does not build up oxygen, it blows off CO₂. Oxygen reserves barely change, but the urge to breathe is reduced.

questions.question: The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects:

options.text: the middle ear with the paranasal sinuses
the middle ear with the inner ear
the middle ear with the nasopharynx
the inner ear with the nasopharynx

questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. It allows pressure equalisation in the middle ear — critical for divers on descent.

questions.question: A consequence of forced over-breathing (hyperventilation) is:

options.text: a drop in carbon dioxide level in the body
a build-up of carbon dioxide in the body
a drop in oxygen level in the body
a build-up of oxygen in the body

questions.explanation: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂ and lowers its level in the blood. This is dangerous on breath-hold dives — the diver may not feel the urge to breathe and can lose consciousness.

questions.question: Equalisation of middle-ear pressure is achieved by:

options.text: opening the orifices of the paranasal sinuses
closing the orifices of the auditory (Eustachian) tubes
opening the orifices of the auditory (Eustachian) tubes

questions.explanation: Middle-ear pressure is equalised by opening the Eustachian tubes (Valsalva manoeuvre, swallowing, jaw movement). On descent the pressure must be equalised continuously.

questions.question: When breathing compressed air, the onset of nitrogen narcosis (rapture of the deep) typically occurs at a depth of:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen narcosis on air typically sets in around 30–40 m. Individual susceptibility varies and may be amplified by other factors.

questions.question: Nitrogen narcosis is caused by:

options.text: an elevated partial pressure of oxygen
pressure of equipment on the carotid arteries

questions.explanation: Nitrogen narcosis is caused mainly by nitrogen (a narcotic effect) and can be amplified by elevated CO₂. Helium has no narcotic effect.

questions.question: During time underwater, the fastest tissue to on-gas with nitrogen is:
questions.explanation: Blood on-gasses with nitrogen the fastest because it is in direct contact with the alveoli. Fast tissues (brain, heart) also on-gas quickly thanks to good perfusion.

questions.question: Residual nitrogen:

options.text: is the amount of nitrogen needed to fully saturate a given tissue
off-gasses from the body for many hours after surfacing
is the nitrogen dissolved in the tissues from immersion until ascent at the prescribed rate begins
is off-gassed from the body during decompression stop(s)

questions.explanation: Residual nitrogen is nitrogen dissolved in the tissues after a dive. It off-gasses for many hours after surfacing — that is why the surface interval before another dive or before flying matters.

questions.question: During time underwater, the slowest tissue to on-gas with nitrogen is:
questions.explanation: Ligaments, tendons and bones (slow tissues) on-gas the slowest because of poor perfusion. They are at risk on long or repetitive dives.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: On descent, nitrogen is distributed by blood throughout the body.
Compared with most body structures, fatty tissue dissolves about five times more nitrogen.
Residual nitrogen off-gasses from the body for many hours after surfacing.
Tissues that on-gas faster on descent off-gas more slowly on ascent.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — tissues that on-gas quickly also off-gas quickly (fast tissues). Slow tissues both on-gas and off-gas slowly.

questions.question: The normal average core body temperature is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal core body temperature is approximately 37 °C (36.5–37.5 °C). Temperatures above 42 °C or below 28 °C are life-threatening.

questions.question: Mark the incorrect statement:

options.text: The auditory (Eustachian) tubes connect the middle-ear cavities with the nasopharynx.
Middle-ear pressure equalisation requires opening the Eustachian tube orifices.
The balance organ is located in the inner ear.
In a healthy person, the paranasal sinuses are not connected to the airways.

questions.explanation: Statement (d) is incorrect — in a healthy person the paranasal sinuses are freely connected to the nasal cavity (and therefore to the airways).

questions.question: Pressure equalisation in the paranasal sinuses:

options.text: requires opening the auditory (Eustachian) tube orifices
is automatic in a healthy person
is necessary only when diving with scuba
is provided by the elasticity of the sinus walls

questions.explanation: In a healthy person, pressure equalisation in the paranasal sinuses is automatic thanks to their free connection to the nasal cavity. Problems arise with a cold or sinusitis.

questions.question: Vasodilation is a body response that protects against:
questions.explanation: Vasodilation is a protective response against overheating — more blood flows to the body surface and heat is dissipated to the surroundings. In cold, the vessels constrict instead (vasoconstriction).
